description: We are a team of passionate students exploring the intersection of space science, AI, and technology. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we're developing a Space Mission Design Game that makes space exploration interactive, strategic, and educational. We're interested in AI/ML, astrophysics, programming, and game design. We're looking for creative teammates skilled in game development, UI/UX, Python, JavaScript, 3D modelling, and space science. Let's innovate beyond Earth!
summary:
Blue Horizon: First Light is a 3D space-exploration game in which players plan and fly a science expedition from the Moon to Mars and back. Players choose a rover’s battery, power source and instruments within a budget. They then land the ship by hand, explore the lunar south pole, scan signals and build a research station. On Mars, they drill a sample of layered delta rock and shelter from a dust storm. They must then fly the sample home for it to count.

The game makes real mission-design trade-offs into choices players feel. Every kilogram of equipment or fuel changes the ship’s fuel budget through the rocket equation. Mars gets less sunlight for solar power, and scans give evidence with a confidence level rather than certain answers. The lunar terrain comes from NASA LOLA elevation data, and the science goals are inspired by Artemis, VIPER and Perseverance. Real facts are clearly labelled apart from game fiction.

Mission planning is usually invisible to the public. Blue Horizon lets students experience how scientists plan missions, in a forgiving game with retries and checkpoints.
details:
Blue Horizon: First Light is a 3D mission design and exploration game built around a practical problem: reaching a scientific target is only useful if the mission can collect evidence and return safely with its limited resources.

Players plan an expedition, explore the Moon and Mars, investigate signals, manage power and fuel, and bring their findings home. Equipment choices have consequences. Extra instruments improve scientific capability but add mass. Solar power reduces dependence on carried supplies but becomes less useful in shadow or during a Martian dust storm. A promising discovery can force players to decide whether to investigate further, recharge, or preserve enough energy for the return journey.

The game includes a traverse planning lab that uses NASA LRO/LOLA lunar elevation and Mars Global Surveyor/MOLA Martian elevation. Players compare routes under chosen battery, slope and reserve constraints. The planner estimates the energy needed for both the outward and return journeys and explains why a candidate meets or exceeds those limits. It addresses a real mission-planning concern through a simplified educational model; it is not a flight-validated navigation system.

The fictional “First Light” campaign turns those decisions into a playable Moon → Mars → Moon-base expedition. Players control a rover and spacecraft, attempt landings with optional assistance, scan sites, analyse samples, establish research equipment and deliver evidence. Scientific findings can remain uncertain or be ruled out, helping players understand that disproving a suspected resource is also a useful result. Mars dust storms affect visibility and solar charging, while gentle rover damage introduces the consequences of hard impacts. Checkpoints, free repairs and forgiving landing retries keep these lessons accessible.

Short cinematics introduce the planning problem, present the player’s selected route using its calculated results, and explain the expedition’s outcome. An in-game science reference connects mission decisions to NASA material, including lunar polar ice observations, Jezero delta imagery and rover observations of Martian dust. Sources and credits are available inside the game. Measured elevation is distinguished from compressed terrain, fictional deposits, equipment balancing and illustrative weather.

We developed Blue Horizon in Godot using GDScript, with custom 3D environments, interface elements and shaders. The browser export uses WebAssembly, HTML and JavaScript, alongside a Windows version. GitHub supports collaboration and version control, and Codex and Claude Code assisted development, debugging and documentation. AI contributions are acknowledged. Players need a computer, keyboard and mouse; no specialist hardware is required.

Its creative approach combines exploration and discovery with engineering decisions that remain visible throughout the experience. Players do not receive only a final score: they see how their choices affect mobility, evidence quality, power availability and the ability to return.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, clear NASA attribution, accessibility, browser performance, readable controls and a manageable development scope. The intended impact is to make mission trade-offs understandable through experience, giving students a way to ask, try and revise: “Can this mission achieve its objective—and can it still get home?”
